papers.title: A large EEG dataset for studying cross-session variability in motor imagery brain-computer interface.
papers.key_finding: In 25 participants recorded across five days, reported classification accuracy was 68.8% within-session, 53.7% cross-session, and 78.9% with cross-session adaptation.
papers.counterevidence_or_limitation: The abstract reports benchmark results but does not describe a matched-training-volume control that isolates adaptation from the benefit of adding training data. Dataset results are not a test of sustained home use.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Provides a direct cross-session benchmark and supports testing adaptation on held-out sessions. To separate adaptation benefit from data-volume benefit, compare adaptation with a control trained on the same number of trials, using equivalent session splits and evaluation.

papers.title: Improving inter-session performance via relevant session-transfer for multi-session motor imagery classification.
papers.key_finding: Relevant-session transfer, which uses selected EEG data from a previous session, improved performance by 2.29% on the Shu dataset (p < 0.001) and up to 6.37% on a gait-related motor-imagery dataset compared with self-calibration.
papers.counterevidence_or_limitation: The abstract does not report a matched-volume comparison, so the reported improvement does not isolate session-aware transfer from the effect of adding training data. It does not establish home-use or clinical benefit.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Directly compares prior-session transfer with current-session self-calibration. A NeuroWeave control should match the number of training trials between cumulative adaptation and a non-session-selective data-volume baseline, then evaluate on the same future sessions.

papers.title: An adaptive session-incremental broad learning system for continuous motor imagery EEG classification.
papers.key_finding: The proposed adaptive session-incremental system was evaluated on BCI Competition IV-2a with two sessions and IV-2b with five sessions, reporting average decoding accuracies of 79.89% and 87.04%, respectively; the study also evaluated kappa and forgetting rate.
papers.counterevidence_or_limitation: The abstract does not provide a frozen-decoder comparison or matched-volume control, and the reported averages alone do not establish that adaptation improved performance on an unseen future session.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Its sequential-session framing and use of a forgetting metric are relevant to cumulative adaptation. NeuroWeave can test both future-session accuracy and whether adding sessions harms earlier-session performance, while matching training volume in a comparator.

papers.title: Towards subject-centered co-adaptive brain-computer interfaces based on backward optimal transport.
papers.key_finding: The study describes backward optimal transport for across-session motor-imagery BCI use without classifier retraining and evaluates a supportive backward adaptation approach using real and simulated data. Adaptation effort correlated significantly with Riemannian distinctiveness metrics.
papers.counterevidence_or_limitation: The abstract does not report a numerical decoder-accuracy gain or a matched-data-volume comparison; its main reported result concerns the adaptation-effort metric.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Shows a way to adapt data across sessions without retraining the classifier, helping distinguish representation alignment from simply accumulating more decoder-training samples. NeuroWeave could include such a comparator alongside frozen and cumulative retrained decoders.

papers.title: Dynamic source domain selection: An adaptive EEG transfer learning framework for mitigating negative transfer.
papers.key_finding: The paper describes negative-transfer risk when source and target domains are dissimilar and evaluates dynamic source selection on three motor-imagery EEG datasets, reporting accuracies of 78.78%, 82.11%, and 78.19%, with improvements over baseline algorithms ranging from 0.13% to 27.7%.
papers.counterevidence_or_limitation: The abstract focuses on cross-domain and subject variability, not a longitudinal held-out future-session comparison. Its reported improvements do not quantify how often transfer itself reduces performance or isolate data-volume effects.
papers.neuroweave_relevance: Contextualizes why adaptation should not be assumed to help every session: source-target mismatch may make transfer risky. NeuroWeave should report per-participant and per-session gains and losses and compare transferred data with a same-volume control.
